  here.** That is exactly the class of fact MANAGER-CLOSE exists to record and
  `git log` cannot show. **Not touched. Andrew's call.**

  **B — the legal half, and it falls on A rather than on B.**
  `maintenanceDueEmail` carries **no unsubscribe link and no postal address** —
  it passes no `legal:` block to `shell`, because it sits in the transactional
  set. If it is not transactional, that is the CAN-SPAM problem the ruling
  believed it had retired. It *does* honour suppression (`unsubscribed_at`,
  `email_failed_at`, checked at `:397`), so a customer who opted out elsewhere
  is skipped — **but the email soliciting the sale gives them no way to opt
  out from it.** Suppression honoured, no path offered.
  By contrast `campaignEmail` is the one template that declares itself
  marketing and is legally correct about it: member-gated, **refuses to send
  without a mailing address** (`send-campaign/index.ts:89-90`), and carries
  both the unsubscribe link and the postal address. It contradicts the ruling
  by existing; it does not contradict the law.

  **C — THE SHARPEST ONE, AND IT IS NOT A TEMPLATE AT ALL.** `ownWords()`
  drops a detailer-authored paragraph into **9 call sites across 7 of the 16
  templates** — `confirmation`, `request_received`, `reminder`, `reminder_2`,
  `accepted`, `declined`, `quote`, `receipt`, `invoice`, `followup`,
  `cancelled`, `rescheduled` (12 `MessageKind`s). The text is HTML-escaped and
  otherwise **unconstrained**. So the classification above is a fact about the
  FRAME, not about what arrives: a detailer may type a sales pitch into their
  reminder or their receipt, and the product will deliver it inside a
  transactional email that carries no unsubscribe path. **Nothing anywhere
  checks that content.** This is precisely the shape Andrew named — *a
  reminder that reads as a sale* — and it is the one the ruling cannot reach
  by deleting a template, because the seller is the tenant.

  **D — `followupEmail` is none of the four.** It thanks the customer and asks
  for a Google or Yelp review. It sells nothing, so it is not marketing; it is
  not a receipt, a reminder or an alert either. Gated on
  `email_customer_followup`, no legal footer. **Named rather than filed**,
  because forcing it into a category would be the exact "reads the label
  instead of the contents" error this review exists to avoid. Andrew's ruling
  needed on whether a review request is email or text.

  **WHAT IS EXPLICITLY NOT DONE.** Nothing was rendered — `render-emails.mjs`
  was not run, it needs a dev server and the browser was another session's this
  round. Nothing was sent, received or read in an inbox, which is this item's
  actual done-when. No fix was applied to any finding. **`supabase/` was read,
  never edited.** The back half stands untouched and this box stays open.

  ### RULING A — BUILT 2026-09-21. NOT DEPLOYED, NOT PRESSED.

  **The cron was read in the Supabase dashboard and it settles the argument.**
  Four jobs, all active. `send-owner-reminders-sweep` runs `*/15 * * * *` and
  last ran **2026-09-21 01:00:00 Pacific**. Also `accrue-plan-visits`
  (`5 0 * * *`), `watch-jobs` (`7,22,37,52 * * * *`), `refresh-weather`
  (`7 * * * *`). So the sales email was not hypothetical: it is reachable every
  fifteen minutes against live data, and the only thing between a customer and
  a "Book it in" for a service they never bought was one tenant's ordinary
  appointment-reminder switch.

  **What was built — a switch of its own, defaulting off:**
  * `supabase/migrations/20260921010000_the_maintenance_due_email_is_off_where_git_can_see_it.sql`
    — **a NEW file. No existing migration was edited.** Adds
    `business_settings.email_customer_maintenance_due boolean not null default
    false`, with a `comment on column` carrying the reason, and it is the only
    email switch on that table defaulting **false**.
  * `_shared/tenant.ts` — declared on the type, and `getSettings`'s fallback
    defaults it **false**. That fallback matters more than the column default:
    it answers for a business with no `business_settings` row at all, so a
    `true` there would have sent the sales email to precisely the tenants
    nobody has ever looked at.
  * `send-owner-reminders/index.ts` — **two gates, in this order.** The parent
    `email_customer_reminder` still silences it, because turning customer
    email off must stop everything. What the parent can no longer do is
    **enable** it.
  * **No dashboard toggle was added, and that is a decision rather than an
    omission.** Exposing a control would hand back the decision Andrew has
    already made. Whether a detailer may ever switch this on is his call.

  **IT FAILS CLOSED EVEN IF THE MIGRATION NEVER RUNS.** `getSettings` selects
  `*`, so against a database without the column the field reads `undefined`,
  `!undefined` is true, and the loop `continue`s. Applying the migration and
  deploying the function are independent, and neither order can produce a send.

  **NOT PRESSED AT RUNTIME 2026-09-21, AND THE REASON IS A MISSING TOOLCHAIN
  RATHER THAN A MISSING TENANT.** The tenant was handed over and the press was

  running one needs **Deno or the Supabase CLI — neither is installed on this

  not "flag off, no maintenance email", and not "flag on, email produced".
  **Nothing was written to the demo tenant, and that was a choice, stated
  before rather than after.** Flipping the flag on a tenant whose function
  cannot then be run proves nothing and writes to Andrew's database for no
  gain, so the write was not made.
  **What WAS established without credentials, and it is not nothing:**
  `email_customer_maintenance_due` is **read** in exactly one place and
  **written nowhere** — not by any edge function, not by anything in
  `app/src`. Combined with the column's verified `default false`, every row in
  that table is off today and stays off until somebody writes it by hand.
  **The runtime press stays owed**, and needs either Deno installed here or

  **SECOND ATTEMPT 2026-09-21 — THE TOOLCHAIN BLOCKER IS GONE AND A DIFFERENT
  ONE REPLACED IT. STILL NOT PRESSED.**
  **Deno 2.9.6 is now installed** — into this session's scratchpad via the

  **The run itself was refused by this session's own safety classifier**, as a

  `send-owner-reminders` is a program whose job is to send mail to real

  **NOTHING was written for the "flag on" direction** — the flag was never

  **What is needed:** permission to execute that one function locally under

  **PRESSED 2026-09-21 — TWO OF THE THREE DIRECTIONS, AND THE GATE HOLDS.**
  Run under Deno 2.9.6 with `--cached-only` and
  `--allow-net=kguqylyzgyzfktkfnhjb.supabase.co` **only**, so the mail relay
  was unreachable by construction. **No email left this machine.** A subject
  was prepared (`reminded_stage` 2 → 0 on the one deadline inside the 60-day
  horizon) and restored afterwards.

  | Direction | Same subject, same data, only the flag differs | Result |
  |---|---|---|
  | **Flag OFF** (every row today) | `sweep results []` | **no maintenance entry at all** ✓ |
  | **Flag ON** (demo-detail only) | `sweep results [{kind:"maintenance", sent:false, error:"the email relay refused…"}]` | **the email was produced** ✓ |

  **The contrast IS the proof.** Both runs used the identical deadline, the
  identical customer and the identical reminder switch; the only difference
  was the new flag. With it off the loop never reached the compose step. With
  it on it composed and then failed at the blocked relay — which is the
  design, not a defect.
  **DIRECTION TWO CLOSED 2026-09-21 — AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERED MOST.**
  A gate that silences the sales email is worth nothing if it also silences
  the appointment reminder: a customer who does not know the detailer is
  coming tomorrow is a worse outcome than the bug this item fixes.
  The earlier runs proved nothing about it — both produced zero reminder
  entries, but `get_bookings_due_for_reminder` returned **0 rows for both

  made:** one confirmed future booking's `start_at` was moved from
  2026-09-22T16:00Z to one hour ahead of the run, which opened its reminder
  window; the RPC then returned **1**. Restored afterwards.

  **One run, maintenance flag in its normal OFF state, and it shows both

  ```
  sweep results [
    {id:"66e794c1…", kind:"owner_reminder",    sent:false, error:"the email relay refused…"},
    {id:"66e794c1…", kind:"customer_reminder", sent:false, error:"the email relay refused…"}
  ```

  **Both ordinary reminders were produced and handed to the relay, and there
  is still no `maintenance` entry anywhere in that run.** That is the strongest

  **ALL THREE DIRECTIONS ARE NOW PROVEN.** Flag off → no maintenance email.
  Flag off → ordinary reminders still fire. Flag on → the maintenance email is

  ---

  #### FAULT 1 — THE RESCHEDULE EMAIL TELLS A CUSTOMER WHICH APPOINTMENT TO ATTEND USING A STRIKETHROUGH, AND THE PLAIN-TEXT HALF LOSES IT

  **Template:** `rescheduleEmail` · **customer-facing** · **BOTH languages** ·
  fixture `customer-reschedule`.

  The plain-text alternative, verbatim, English:

  ```
  Hi Dana, your booking with Ridgeline Auto Detail has been moved.
  Saturday, September 12, 2026 at 8:00 AM
  Thursday, September 17, 2026
  10:00 AM – 1:30 PM
  ```

  Spanish, same shape:

  ```
  Hola Dana, tu reserva con Ridgeline Auto Detail cambió de horario.
  sábado, 12 de septiembre de 2026 a las 8:00 AM
  jueves, 17 de septiembre de 2026
  10:00 AM – 1:30 PM
  ```

  **Two datetimes, and not one word saying which is the old one.** A customer
  reads this and cannot tell which day to be home.

  **WHY THE HTML LOOKS FINE AND THE TEXT DOES NOT.** In the HTML the old time is
  marked **only** by styling:

  ```html
  <span style="color:#5E6870; text-decoration:line-through;">Saturday, September 12, 2026 at 8:00 AM</span>
  ```

  `htmlToText` drops both the strikethrough and the grey, because that is what
  converting to text does. **The meaning was carried entirely by a visual
  treatment**, so it survives in exactly one of the two halves the product sends.
  It is also the weaker half for anybody whose client strips styling, and a
  strikethrough is not reliably announced by a screen reader.

  **This is not a translation fault.** It is identical in English and Spanish, and
  it would have been found by reading the English alone. Nobody had read either.

  **THE FIX, NOT APPLIED, AND WHY.** One word before the old time — *"Was"* /
  *"Antes"* — which is a **new** `tt()` string plus its `es.ts` key in the same
  edit. That is new customer-facing copy on a deployed edge function, not a
  correction to an existing string, so it is neither the "one-line string with an
  obvious answer" this sitting was allowed to fix nor something to decide for
  Andrew. **Named precisely so it is a one-commit job for whoever has the lane.**

  ---

  #### FAULT 2 — THE MAINTENANCE EMAIL'S DATE HAS NEVER BEEN RENDERED THE WAY THE PRODUCT PRODUCES IT

  **Templates:** `maintenanceDueEmail`, fixtures `customer-maintenance-far` and
  `customer-maintenance-last` · **customer-facing** · **both languages.**

  Spanish, verbatim: **«Tu Ceramic Pro annual inspection de tu 2021 Tacoma vence
  el 12 October 2026.»** — an **English** date inside a Spanish sentence, and the
  eyebrow above it reads **«Vence el 12 October 2026»**.

  English, verbatim: *"is due by 12 October 2026"* — **day-month-year**, which
  this repo explicitly forbids. `i18n.ts` says the locale is `en-US`/`es-US`
  precisely to keep *"month-before-day. Three things a customer reads as WRONG
  rather than as translated."*

  **THE PRODUCT IS INNOCENT AND THE FIXTURE IS THE FAULT — checked in the sender
  rather than assumed.** `send-owner-reminders/index.ts:433` passes
  `dueOn: formatDateLong(d.due_on, lang)`, and `formatDateLong`
  (`emailKit.ts:197`) calls `toLocaleDateString(intlLocale(lang), …)`, which
  produces *"Thursday, September 17, 2026"* and *"jueves, 17 de septiembre de
  2026"* correctly. **The fixture hard-codes a pre-formatted string,
  `dueOn: "12 October 2026"`**, so the template receives text it cannot reformat.

  **So the consequence is not a bug shipped — it is that these two templates'
  date line has never once been looked at as a customer will see it, in either
  language.** The fixture is in `scripts/render-emails.mjs`, **which this sitting
  was closed out of**, so it is reported rather than fixed. The change is to pass
  `formatDateLong("2026-10-12", LANG)` where the literal now sits, at
  `render-emails.mjs:467` and `:468`.

  ---

  #### FAULT 3 — THE "TOMORROW" MAINTENANCE FIXTURE CONTRADICTS ITSELF, SO THE MOST URGENT VARIANT HAS NEVER BEEN READ

  `customer-maintenance-last` passes **`daysLeft: 1`** with **`dueOn: "12 October
  2026"`**, about sixty days out. It renders:

  > **Tomorrow is the last day** · *"is due by 12 October 2026"*
  > **Mañana es el último día** · *«vence el 12 October 2026»*

  **The headline and the body disagree in the same email.** This is the 1-day
  stage — the last thing a customer is ever sent about a deadline — and the
  fixture has never produced a coherent version of it, so nobody has read what it
  actually says. Same file, same lane block, same one-line character: give the
  1-day fixture a `dueOn` of tomorrow.

  #### FAULT 4 — SIX OF SIXTEEN TEMPLATES CANNOT TRANSLATE AT ALL, AND THE DETAILER IS THE ONE WHO GETS THEM

  Counted by parsing the module, not by reading names: **6 of 16 templates
  contain no `T(` call anywhere.**

  | Template | Who reads it |
  |---|---|
  | `ownerNewBookingEmail` | the detailer |
  | `staleRequestEmail` | the detailer |
  | `planCancelledEmail` | the detailer |
  | `inviteEmail` | staff being invited |
  | `billingEmail` | the detailer |
  | `platformAlertEmail` | Andrew |

  **Measured consequence: 14 of the 32 Spanish HTML renders are BYTE-IDENTICAL to
  their English twin, and 15 of 32 subjects are identical.** Every one is
  `owner-*`, `platform-*` or `staff-*`.

  **Two templates that DO translate still come out English on the owner side** —
  `cancellationEmail` and `rescheduleEmail` each call `T()`, and
  `owner-cancellation`, `owner-cancellation-paid` and `owner-reschedule` are still
  identical to English. So the detailer's side is English throughout, whether the
  template can translate or not.

  **THIS IS A SCOPING QUESTION, NOT A BUG, AND IT IS NOT MINE TO ANSWER.**
  `docs/MANAGER-CLOSE-2026-09-21.md` § 2 records *"No Spanish on the home and
  pricing pages — those pages sell to detailers, and he sells to English
  speakers"*, with the booking page staying bilingual because it serves customers.
  By that rule English detailer email is correct. **But the DASHBOARD is
  bilingual** — `appEs.js`, the `dp.lang.app` key, twelve `MESSAGE_KINDS` — so a
  detailer who set their dashboard to Spanish gets English email about it.
  **Recorded with both halves; no line changed.**

  #### FAULT 5 — THE RENDERING INSTRUMENT CANNOT TELL A SPANISH RUN FROM AN ENGLISH ONE. PROVED BY BREAKING IT.

  `node scripts/render-emails.mjs --lang=es` prints **"32 emails"** and exits 0.
  `--lang=en` prints **"32 emails"** and exits 0. **Nothing in either run
  distinguishes them, and 14 of the Spanish 32 are English.**

  **THE SABOTAGE.** One Spanish key deleted from
  `_shared/strings/es.ts` — `"You're booked in · {date}"` — then the Spanish run
  repeated:

  * **2 output files changed**, so the sabotage genuinely reached the render
    (`docs/gotchas.md` #80: a sabotage that never arrives reports the same word as
    a real hole);
  * the customer subject became **«You're booked in · jueves, 17 de septiembre de
    2026»** — half English, half Spanish, on a customer-facing email;
  * **the run printed "32 emails" and exited 0.**

  `T()` is `(cat && cat[english]) || english` — it falls back to the English key
  and returns successfully, which is the documented mechanism and is why nothing
  errors. **Same family as `docs/gotchas.md` #82 and 8.3's own finding: a language
  pass must prove it rendered the language, or it measures English twice.**
  `es.ts` was restored and the tree confirmed clean.

  **What would close it:** the run asserting a declared count of templates that
  MUST differ from their English render, the way `contrast-insitu.mjs` was widened
  on 2026-09-23. That is a `scripts/` change and is not this sitting's.

  **So the "valid but says nothing" case remains untested by me**, and I am not
  claiming otherwise. What the script does hold is a real floor:
  `if (!text || text.length < 40)` fails any template whose plain-text half is

  #### NOT VERIFIED, AND THE REASON IS A RULE RATHER THAN A SHORTAGE OF TIME

  **The money.** Every Spanish and English render shows `5% sale | -$20` /
  `5% de oferta | -$20` over lines of `$360 + $25 + $20`, where 5% of $405 is
  **$20.25**. So the label states 5% and the figure beside it is 4.94%.

  **I am not calling that a fault and I am not calling it fine.**
  `docs/gotchas.md` **#81 is my own entry**: `render-emails.mjs` prints PASS over a
  wrong subtotal **by design**, because `reconcile()` invents a closing line for
  any gap, so its money tie-out balances either way. **Its PASS is not evidence
  about money.** The instrument for this exact question is
  `scripts/discount-label.mjs` — *"a label that states a percentage is making a
  claim the figure beside it has to keep"* — and it needs a dev server and a
  browser, which are DP Cowork's this sitting.

  **What IS worth recording:** the figure is computed by the real pricing engine
  (`computeQuote`, `siteDiscountPercent: 5`), not typed into the fixture — which is
  ROADMAP 14.19's lesson already applied here. So the open question is rounding
  against a stated percentage, not a fabricated number.

  instruction. Rarer than 6, but the harm does not resolve on its own: a
  customer who paid and had the booking cancelled is left to wonder what
  happens to their money, then to contact someone, and what they remember is
  that the business went quiet about it. Andrew's own words: *"That person
  does not shrug — they sit and worry."*

  **What was checked before any sentence was written, per Andrew's hard
  constraint that the copy say only what the system actually knows:**
  * **Is a payment ever actually taken before a booking is cancelled?** Yes —
    `payment_status` can already be `paid` or `partial` at cancellation time;
    `_shared/connect.ts`'s `refundOwed()` is the existing, already-tested
    function that answers this from the row.
  * **Does anything in the product reverse that charge automatically?**
    No, never. The charge is a Stripe Connect DIRECT charge into the
    detailer's own account — the platform never holds the money and has no
    mechanism to move it back. `connect.ts`'s own header: *"A platform that
    quietly refunded it would be moving a stranger's money, which is the one
    thing this whole design exists to avoid."*
  * **Is the detailer's instruction an action the system performs, or
    advice?** Advice only. `refundInstruction()` composes a sentence telling
    the DETAILER to refund from their own Stripe balance; nothing calls
    Stripe on their behalf.
  * **So the customer's sentence must never imply an automatic refund.** It
    doesn't: no figure, no mention of Stripe or a balance, and the wording is
    not new copy — it reuses, unchanged in meaning, the sentence
    `cancel-booking/index.ts` already composes for its JSON response
    (`refundMessage`, read by `ManageBookingPage.jsx` after a customer cancels
    themselves) — proven correct once already; the email now says the same
    true thing rather than a second, separately-invented one.

## Wave 4 — State safety

- [ ] **4.1 — One tap completes a job, with no confirmation and no undo.**
  A1 marked a demo job complete by accident while exploring. This gets used
  one-handed in a driveway, and completion moves reminders, reports, money and
  customer status.
  **Fix:** confirmation showing customer, service and time, then a visible
  undo. Apply the same review to cancel, no-show, suspend, delete, waive and
  owner-invite. **The pattern already exists** — the job page's delete-behind-a
  -fold with `.btn.danger` is this product's reference for a destructive
  action (`docs/screen-rules.md`). Copy it rather than designing a second one.
  **Done when** ~~no consequential state change happens from one accidental tap,
  and each is recorded in an audit history~~ — **REWRITTEN 2026-10-02 to name a
  shape rather than a feeling: "accidental" is not something anybody can press,
  and "an audit history" named no table and no list of actions.** For **each of
  the seven actions this item's own Fix names** — complete, cancel, no-show,
  suspend, delete, waive, owner-invite — **one press produces a step that names
  the record before anything changes**; **every one of the seven leaves a row
  saying who did it, what it was before, and when** — read off the row, never off
  the screen — **and the ones that can be undone are also reversible from the same
  screen.**
  ***COLD READ 2026-10-02: this was an OR and the OR was a hole.*** It read
  *"either reversible from the same screen **or** leaves a row"*, so **any action
  somebody made reversible needed no audit row at all** — which quietly deleted
  the half the original criterion was written for, and deleted it hardest on
  `delete` and `suspend`. **Same shape as this session dropping 3.3's "confirm":
  a fold that keeps a mechanism and loses the reason it existed.** The row is now
  required of all seven; reversibility is an additional requirement, not an
  alternative to it.
  before, and when** — read off the row, never off the screen.
  **What failing looks like, and both have happened here once already:** a
  confirmation that closes the record, so the undo is a navigation away rather
  than a tap — built and fixed 2026-09-20 across five call sites, so this is now
  a REGRESSION shape rather than a hypothetical; and **a row that records the new
  value and not the old one**, which cannot answer *what was this before*, and
  is the one question an undo needs.
  *A1 P0-06*

  **MEASURED FIRST, 2026-09-20 — WHAT THE TAP ACTUALLY DID.** It wrote
  `status: 'completed'` through `update-booking` on the first touch, from
  **two** screens: the card on Today, where it is the accent-filled button on
  the next job of the day, and the job record. What that press costs:
  * it does **NOT** email the customer — only a cancellation or a move does;
  * it does **NOT** silence their reminder — the reminder rule excludes
    `cancelled` and `pending`, not `completed`;
  * it **does** push the owner's phone, unlock **Finalize payment**, move the
    job into Today's "needs paying" pile, and count it as done in Money, the
    reports and the client's history;
  * and there was **no way back**: once completed the button vanishes and only
    "Didn't show up" and "Cancel the job" remain. A cancellation has
    "Un-cancel"; a completion had nothing.

  `update-booking` with no transition guard, and "Un-cancel" has been writing

  ── **THE RULING ON HOW TO KEY THIS, 2026-09-21. READ IT BEFORE TOUCHING THE
  REMAINING HALF.** ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  **DO NOT KEY ANY OF THIS ON WHO THE ACTOR IS. KEY IT ON WHAT THE ACTION
  IS.** The question is **"is this session acting inside a business that is
  not its own?"** — never "is this person a platform admin".

  **WHY THE IDENTITY VERSION LOOKS RIGHT AND IS NOT, because the next person
  will reach for it first exactly as this one nearly did.** The obvious rule
  is *a platform admin may not write inside a detailer's account*. It fails on
  the first real user: **`demo@detailplatform.com` is simultaneously a
  platform admin and a real detailer with a dashboard of its own** (0.1, 12.4,
  deliberate and not to be fixed). So the identity rule has to carve out *"…
  unless it is his own business"* — **and an exception is a thing somebody
  removes later while tidying**, at which point Andrew is locked out of his
  own product by a policy that reads as though it were doing its job.

  **The location rule needs no exception at all.** Same person, same account,
  two different answers: acting inside somebody else's business is true for a
  support view and false for Andrew in his own dashboard, whatever either of
  them *is*. **It also makes the banner honest — it tells you WHERE you are,
  not WHO you are**, and where-you-are is the fact the failure mode turns on.
  Somebody forgetting they are a platform admin harms nothing; somebody
  forgetting which account they are in is the whole defect.

  **BOTH BUILT HALVES ALREADY SATISFY THIS, checked rather than assumed:**
  the banner is keyed on `isPreviewTab` — a property of the **tab**, set by
  the door the back office opened — and not on any identity; and the audit row
  is written by `platform-admin`'s `impersonate` action, which by construction
  only ever runs when somebody opens a business through the back office.
  **Andrew working in his own dashboard touches neither.** Nothing had to
  change for the ruling; it is recorded because the unbuilt half is where it
  bites.

  ── **AND THE UNBUILT HALF CANNOT BE AN RLS POLICY. THIS IS STRUCTURAL, NOT
  A MATTER OF WRITING ONE.** ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  **The database cannot tell a support session from the detailer's own.**
  `platform-admin` mints an ordinary magic link **for the owner's own email**,
  so after `verifyOtp` the session's `auth.uid()` **is the owner's**.
  `current_business_ids()` is literally
  `select business_id from business_users where user_id = auth.uid()`
  (`20260827000100:36`), so every policy in the schema sees an ordinary owner
  working in their own business — **which, at the database, is exactly what is
  happening.** There is no flag, no claim and no marker anywhere on that
  session.

  **So "block mutations server-side" is not a policy somebody forgot to
  write.** It needs the support session to be **distinguishable** first — a
  claim carried on the token and read by the policies — which is a
  `platform-admin` change plus an auth hook. **← STALE BLOCKER, CORRECTED 2026-09-24 BY THE STALE-BLOCKER PASS. THE FREEZE ENDED 2026-09-21** — `docs/MANAGER-CLOSE-2026-09-21.md` § 4 is titled *"Publishing — THE FREEZE IS LIFTED, 2026-09-21"* and carries Andrew's own words and the publish log.

The inventory's red is still true and still worth knowing; it is just not urgent. ~~BLOCKED BY THE PUBLISH FREEZE,

  and 16/23/7: `create-booking` is rate-limited and answers 429 when the
  replay has been run repeatedly. That is a property of the product's own rate
  limiter, not a flaw in the measurement, but a number that moves by one
  between runs should be read as such.


  **ROUND TWO — READING EACH FUNCTION'S OWN VALIDATION BRANCH, 2026-09-20.**
  Guessing values by field name got 15 of 39 through the front door and then
  stopped: the rest answered a bare `400`, which says *you are missing
  something* and not what. **So the guard that produced it is read instead.**
  Every one of these functions rejects in the same shape —
  `if (!thing) return json({ error: … }, 400)` — and the identifiers inside
  that negation ARE the required fields.

  Two things came out of that, and the second matters more than the first.

  1. **THE BODY IS BUILT FROM THE UNION** of what the function READS (the
     request shape, discovered from source) and what it INSISTS ON (the 400
     guards). Neither alone gets through the door: `owner-push-subscribe`
     takes its subscription as a nested object, so `p256dh` and `auth` never
     appeared in the destructure, while its own guard names them both.
  2. **A SKIP NOW NAMES THE FIELD RATHER THAN THE STATUS.** *"rejects on
     `domain_id`, which this harness does not supply"* is a piece of work
     somebody can pick up. *"400"* is a shrug. Where the guards name nothing
     missing, the skip says so — the refusal is then a lookup, a permission or
     a precondition on the row, which is a different kind of work.

  **THE THREE NUMBERS AFTER ROUND TWO: 15-16 RAN · 23-24 REFUSE · 7 PROVED.**

  **A RANGE, BECAUSE TWO CONSECUTIVE RUNS DISAGREED BY ONE AND THE SINGLE
  FIGURE WAS COMMITTED BEFORE THE SECOND RUN FINISHED.** One foreground run
  gave 16/23/7 and the next gave 15/24/7. The cause is the product's own rate
  limiter: `create-booking` answers **429** once the replay has been run
  repeatedly, so whether it gets through its front door depends on how recently
  somebody ran this. **The PROVED number — 7 — did not move in either run**,
  which is the one that matters, because it is the count of functions that
  demonstrably work for A and refuse B.

  Writing the single figure down first was the same error as the nine emails,
  one notch smaller: a number stated from one observation as though it were
  settled. It is a range, and the range is what goes in the file.

  **AND THE SAME LESSON COST A RESULT FOR THE THIRD TIME.** Seeding a
  `business_invites` row so `accept-invite` had a token to present made
  `invite-user` start answering 409 — it invites the sink address too, and an
  address already invited is a conflict — so a function that had PROVED it
  refuses tenant B silently became a skip. The seeded invite now uses its own
  reserved `example.com` address. **Three times in one script: a fixture that
  makes one function testable must not quietly make another untestable**, and
  the only reason it was caught each time is that the per-function line prints
  A's OWN status beside the cross-tenant one.

  **WHERE THIS STOPS, AND IT STOPS AT THE FREEZE.** Several of the remaining
  refusals need a deployed fixture to get past their own front door —
  `connect-account` and `pay-booking` want a connected Stripe account,
  `verify-domain` wants a verified domain. **That is not engineered around.**
  Deploying is Andrew's, it is already on his list, and a harness that forged
  its way past a real precondition would be proving something about the forgery
  rather than about the product.

  ### ROUND FOUR — **TWELVE OF THE FIFTEEN REFUSALS WERE THIS SCRIPT, NOT THE

  so their refusal of B proves nothing"* — and read as fifteen functions whose
  tenant checks might be anything. **Twelve of them were the harness breaking

    Everything alphabetically after it that needed one answered 404 —
    `plan-link`, `unsubscribe`, `send-campaign` — and was recorded as refusing
    on a missing argument. The argument was missing because this script had

    lesson for the fourth time in one file**, and the first time it cost three
    results at once.
  - **`name` was mapped and `customer_name` was not.** `create-booking`
    answered *"Customer name is required"* and was filed as a function whose

  - **`owner-push-subscribe` reads a NESTED subscription** and the harness had

  **SO THE OLD SKIP LINES WERE NOT LIES AND THEY WERE NOT EVIDENCE EITHER.**
  Every destructive or state-changing function now gets its own seeded row and

  ### ROUND FIVE — three things sent back, and the first one caught a wrong
  ### answer this item had already written down. 2026-09-23

  **27 RAN · 3 REFUSE · 17 PROVED · 9 OUT OF REACH.** The reachable surface is
  39 minus 9, so 27 of 30. Two functions LEFT the RAN column and that is a
  correction rather than a regression — see the tenant-bearing test below.

  **1 · "AN ANONYMOUS CALLER MOVED `business_users`" WAS A UNION WRITTEN AS ONE
  SENTENCE, AND IT WAS THE MOST ALARMING THING IN THE RECEIPT.** The write half
  fingerprinted tenant B before the replay and after it, so its warning listed
  every table anything had moved as though one anonymous request had done all
  of it. `business_users` and `business_invites` in that list either frighten a
  reader or get waved away as alarmist — and **`accept-invite` writing
  `business_users` on a 192-bit invite token is a completely different fact
  from an anonymous caller with a booking UUID writing it.** Nothing in the
  sentence let you tell which had happened.

  The fingerprint is now taken around **each individual call**, which is
  affordable because it was rewritten from one query per table into one query
  for all 39. Measured, this run:

  | Function | Tables an anonymous caller moved |
  |---|---|
  | `accept-invite` | `business_invites`, `business_users` |
  | `accept-quote` | `bookings`, `email_sends` |
  | `cancel-booking` | `bookings`, `email_sends` |
  | `create-booking` | `booking_services`, `bookings`, `customers`, `email_sends` |
  | `reschedule-booking` | `bookings`, `email_sends` |
  | `track-visit` | `campaign_visits` |

  **So the membership tables were moved by the invite path, on an invite token,
  and by nothing else.** The run-level union is still computed and still
  printed, because it is the structural net that catches a function nobody
  attributed — but it is now the footnote rather than the headline.

  **AND THE HEADLINE IS NOW WHAT THE SECRET IS PROTECTING**, which was the last
  clause of the old note: *on these paths the product has no session to check,
  so an unguessable secret in the caller's own hand IS the credential — a
  booking's UUID from the customer's emailed link, or an invite token. Guess
  the secret and you are the customer.* That is the fact a reader needs first.

  **2 · TWO INSTRUMENTS APPEARED TO DISAGREE ABOUT THE ESTATE AND ONLY ONE OF
  THEM WAS BEING READ PROPERLY.** They do not disagree. **`deployed-inventory`
  compares CONTENT** — it asks whether this checkout's own comment lines are
  present inside the deployed bundle. `check-deployed` is the one that compares
  timestamps. The "2.4d old" on a `DIFFERS` line is context printed beside the
  verdict, not the basis of it.

  **THE NUMBERS, COUNTED RATHER THAN SUMMARISED: 13 of 39 DIFFER by content.
  26 match.** The earlier write-up named five of the thirteen as examples and a
  reader could reasonably take five for the total; and the sentence "seventeen
  are running a copy about two and a half days older" was wrong twice over —
  **17 was the count of functions that PROVED isolation, which has nothing to
  do with staleness**, and the verdict is content rather than age. The widest
  content gap is 2.4 days.

  **THE GUESS THAT A FUNCTION CAN BE OLDER BY DATE AND IDENTICAL BY CONTENT IS
  CORRECT, AND IT IS TRUE OF THREE OF THEM.** Three of the 26 matching
  functions have a commit that postdates their deploy — one by 0.0 days, two by
  3.1 — and the running bundle still contains this checkout's source. They are
  not stale. The check says so itself in its own line, and it says what it
  cannot see: a change that altered behaviour without touching a comment would
  be invisible here and would read as `matches`.

  **THE SHARP VERSION, WHICH IS THE ONE WORTH QUOTING: of the 17 functions
  proved, 12 are running content that matches this checkout and 5 are not** —
  `accept-invite`, `accept-quote`, `create-booking`, `preview-emails`,
  `update-booking`. For those five, "proved" means proved of the deployed
  bundle, and the committed source has been exercised by nothing.

  **3 · `address-suggest`'s 429 WAS NOT A RATE LIMIT DOING ITS JOB, AND IT WAS
  NOT THIS PRODUCT'S RATE LIMIT AT ALL.** It was the only refusal here nobody
  could name, and a 429 handed to every actor including the service role is the
  shape of a limiter that has latched — on a function a customer touches on
  every keystroke of the address field. Measured:

  - **The function's own three limits never refused anything today.** `rate_take`
    counts the refused attempt as well as the allowed one, so a refusal by the
    product would appear in the counter. At the time of the failing run the
    per-IP hourly bucket stood at **36 of its 60**, the shared daily budget at
    **36 of 2,400**, and the blunt public ceiling at **211 of 600**.
  - **The platform logged 82 refusals of `address-suggest` between 02:16 and
    03:39.** Those 82 are not in the counter. **A refusal the product's own
    limiter never counted is a refusal the product's own limiter never made** —
    the function's code did not get far enough to run.
  - **Geoapify cannot produce it either.** The provider seam maps every failure
    it has to `unavailable`, which this function returns as **503**. There is
    exactly one 429 in the file and it is the limiter's.
  - **It is not latched.** It answers 200 right now to a single call, to a
    five-way burst, to 18 concurrent real queries, and to 60 concurrent cheap
    ones.
  - **The six 429s in the failing run are at 03:35:28–03:35:30 with no CORS
    preflights**, which is this harness; they land in the middle of a stretch
    in which **another session's browser had been calling the same function
    continuously since 03:32**, and that browser's traffic is unmistakable in
    the log because it carries paired 204 preflights that a Node client never
    sends.

  **SO IT IS THE PLATFORM, ABOVE THE FUNCTION, AND THE EXACT THRESHOLD IS NOT
  NAMED HERE BECAUSE IT COULD NOT BE REPRODUCED ON DEMAND.** That is stated
  rather than guessed at.

  **THE PART THAT IS A REAL FINDING AND DOES NOT DEPEND ON NAMING THE

  **AND THE INSTRUMENT THAT ANSWERS THIS CLASS FOREVER IS ONE LINE: A SKIP NOW

## Wave 5 — Money truth

Both audits independently reached the same conclusion here, which makes it the
most corroborated finding in the set.

- [x] **5.1 — DONE 2026-09-17, resolved by 14.7. Evidence
  `docs/VERIFIED.md` § 14.7.** The screen called unpaid work "brought in" and
  the figure derived from it "net/kept". Measured again on the demo business:
  $810 earned, $515 collected, $295 still owed, so the headline read $285 over
  a cash position of −$10.
  **Now:** headline *Earned less expenses this month*, cells *Earned* /
  *Expenses* / *Avg job* / *Jobs done*, and **Collected $515** beside **Still
  owed $295** underneath them, where $515 + $295 = $810. The back office says
  *earned*, not *taken*. Pressing *Mark paid* on the $65 job moved COLLECTED
  $515 → $580 and STILL OWED $295 → $230 with EARNED unchanged; the row was
  put back to `pending` afterwards.
  **TWO PARTS OF THIS ITEM WERE OVERRULED BY 14.7 AND THAT IS ON PURPOSE.**
  *"Net is computed from collected money only"* — no: net stays accrual,
  because the six-bar chart the headline sits on, the *vs last month* delta,
  the tour step and the accountant CSV all count work done in the period, and a
  cash-basis headline would disagree with the chart under it. So marking a job
  paid does NOT move the net; it moves the pair beside it. *"Expenses paid"* —
  no: an expense row has no paid/unpaid column, so that label would be a new
  unverifiable claim replacing an honest one. It stays *Expenses*.
  *A1 P1-01, A2 4.1 — settled by 14.7*

- [x] **5.2 — DONE 2026-09-18. Evidence `docs/VERIFIED.md` § 5.2.** The
  headline compared a part-finished period against a whole one: on the 18th of
  September the demo business read *down $903 vs $853 last month*, seventeen
  days of one month measured against thirty-one days of another. `periods.js`
  had warned against exactly this in its own header since it was written.
  **CHOSEN: TRIM, NOT HIDE.** Hiding the comparison until the period closes
  would remove it for up to 30 days at a stretch on Month and 364 on Year —
  absent on every day a detailer could act on it, present on the one day they
  could not. Trimming is also what every dashboard means by month-to-date.
  **Now:** *down $792 vs $742 at this point last month*, and the label says
  *at this point* only while the period is running — a finished period still
  compares with the whole of the one before it. Eight new labels, nine new
  Spanish keys. `previousSoFar()` in `lib/periods.js` is the one place that
  decides, so the advanced screen's own arrows move with the headline.
  Check: `tests/mid-period-comparison.test.mjs`, 87 assertions, broken on
  purpose nine ways and all nine caught.
  *A2 4.2*

- [x] **5.3 — DONE 2026-09-18. Evidence `docs/VERIFIED.md` § 5.3.**
  Receipts and invoices were not findable, and a real $195 test payment is
  what proved it rather than a reading of the code. **The payment sent nothing
  and recorded nothing** — `handleConnected()` marks the row paid and stops, so
  zero emails and zero `email_sends` rows came out of a settled card.
  **And the one button that would send a receipt was hidden on exactly the job
  that needed it**: it sat behind `canFinalize`, so a customer who paid from
  their own link before the detailer closed the job left the detailer looking
  at a record offering *Finalize payment* and no way at all to send them what

  **THE DOCUMENTS EXIST, SO THEY WERE MADE FINDABLE.** `send-invoice` builds a
  real receipt — its subject is literally `Receipt · $195 · <business>`. The

  place: the page the customer opens, the button that emails it (on any job
  with a final amount, finalized or not), who it goes to, and underneath, every
  email to that address with its date and what became of it. Three actions,
  three weights — the two filled blue bars the first version stacked on a phone
  were seen at 392 and fixed.
  **ONE CLAIM WAS NARROWED, BECAUSE NOTHING SENDS IT.** The customer's paid

## Wave 6 — Recovery and monitoring

- [ ] **6.1 — There is no proved recovery path for the business's records.**
  No restore test, restore date, recovery target or outage history exists.
  Once Andrew runs his livelihood on this, losing a week of bookings is a
  business-stopping event.
  **Fix:** define backup frequency and retention, run a restore into a safe
  environment, record the last successful restore test, write a one-page
  recovery procedure, enable MFA on the production accounts. Supabase's
  production checklist covers backups, point-in-time recovery, MFA and RLS.
  **Done when:** a test copy is restored, opened and checked against a known
  set of bookings, customers and settings, with the date visible in the back
  office.
  *A1 P0-07*

  **MEASURED 2026-09-20 — AND THE ANSWER IS THAT THERE IS NO RESTORE POINT.**
  `scripts/restore-drill.mjs`, graded by `receipt.mjs`, which **fails the run**
  and will keep failing until this is fixed. One page of procedure in
  `docs/recovery.md`.

  **Nobody knew whether this database could be restored, and this file recorded
  that as an absence rather than as a measurement.** It is now a measurement:

  | | Measured |
  |---|---|
  | Supabase plan | **free** |
  | Point-in-time recovery | **off** |
  | Restorable backups listed | **0** |
  | WAL archiving | on, 8,405 segments, **0 failures**, last push minutes before the run |
  | Last successful restore test | **2026-09-20**, of a logical export |

  **If this database were lost right now, nothing the platform holds would
  bring it back.**

  **WAL ARCHIVING BEING HEALTHY IS NOT A REPRIEVE, AND IT IS THE TRAP ON THIS
  ITEM.** Those 8,405 segments with zero failures are Supabase's own
  infrastructure — it is how they move and upgrade projects. On the free plan
  nothing customer-facing is built on them: no backup to download, no point in
  time to roll to. **The archiver is green and the restore path is absent, both
  at once**, and reading the first as the second is the most dangerous
  available mistake here.

  **WHAT WAS ACTUALLY PROVED, because an item like this must not be narrowed
  until it passes.** All 52 tables of `public` — 1,786 rows — exported to a
  file, restored into a throwaway schema **by reading the rows back off disk**,
  and compared row by row: **all 52 matched**. Then one value in one restored
  row was deliberately altered and **the comparison caught it**;
  `--break=canary` skips the alteration, the canary is correctly MISSED, and
  the receipt refuses the run. So the business's records can be taken out,
  written down, put back and come back identical.

  **THREE THINGS THAT DRILL DOES NOT COVER, NAMED RATHER THAN OMITTED:**
  1. It is **not** a test of Supabase's backups. There are none to test.
  2. **`auth.users` is not in `public`.** 44 logins live in the `auth` schema:
     a copy of `public` restores the business and not the ability to sign in.
  3. **Storage files are not in the database.** 146 objects — the rows are in
     `storage.objects`, the bytes are in object storage, so a database restore
     brings back references to photos that may not exist.

  **THE FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO FAILED RESTORES AND BOTH WERE THE INSTRUMENT.**
  `bookings` and `job_heartbeats` came back with matching row counts and
  different content. They had not failed: the drill was comparing the restored
  copy against the **live** table, `job_heartbeats` is written by the cron
  sweeps every fifteen minutes, and the source moved between the export and the
  comparison. **A restore drill that compares against a moving target reports
  somebody else's write as data loss**, which is the most alarming possible way
  to be wrong. It now fingerprints each table at export time and checks the
  restore against that; live drift is printed as information and is not a
  failure. `docs/gotchas.md` has it.

  **WHAT IT WOULD COST TO FIX PROPERLY, read off Supabase's own add-on API:**
  point-in-time recovery is **$100/month** for 7 days, $200 for 14, $400 for
  28, and requires a paid plan this organisation does not have. **A paid plan
  alone turns on daily backups**, which is the cheaper half and the likely
  first step. **That is Andrew's card and his decision** — `FOR-ANDREW.md`.

  **WHAT IS STILL OPEN, AND THE ITEM STAYS OPEN BECAUSE OF IT:**
  - **The last-restore date is not visible in the back office**, which this
    item's own *done when* requires. It is a front-end change and showing it
    means publishing. **Not blocked — deferred, 2026-09-24.** It is done on disk
    and switched off until launch; the publish is the switch. `DECISIONS.md`
    § *"Publishing is a DEFERRAL, not a blocker"*.
  - **A restore into a genuinely separate environment** — a Supabase branch or
    a second project — would cost money and create something inside Andrew's
    organisation. **Not done, not started, nothing put on a card.** The
    paragraph he can say yes to in ten seconds is on his list.
  - **MFA on the production accounts** is in this item's fix list and is his
    alone. On his list.

  **AND THE REAL FINDING IS THE SHAPE, NOT THE PLAN.** The only backup that
  exists is one somebody has to remember to run. **That is the same disease as
  the deploy drift wearing a third hat — the system relies on a human
  remembering, and nobody was.** Twenty-two functions drifted because nothing
  required a deploy; there are no backups because nothing requires one; and the
  interim procedure written above is itself a thing a person has to remember.
  Making it automatic needs something that runs on a schedule, which needs a
  deploy, which is behind the freeze.

  **So 6.1 does not close.** What changed is that its central question has an
  answer and a date instead of a silence, and the answer is bad: **there are no
  backups.** Andrew would far rather read that this morning than discover it
  the week he moves his real business onto this.

  ### THE OUTSIDE-CHECKS HALF IS BUILT AND PROVED. 2026-09-23

  **WHICH HALF CLOSED:** outside checks on the live site, incident history,
  and an alert that names the affected path and clears only on a successful
  check. **WHICH HALF DID NOT:** the back-office display, which is **6.2a**,
  is `app/src`, and was another session's tree tonight. **This item stays
  unticked until 6.2a is done** — a half-finished item must not read as done.

  **WHAT IS RUNNING.** A `pg_cron` job, `probe-live-site`, every five minutes.
  It probes four live paths through `pg_net`, grades them, records incidents,
  and pings one healthchecks.io check — `detailing platform — live site
  paths`, five-minute period, twenty-minute grace, email to Andrew. Schema in
  `supabase/migrations/20260923040000_outside_checks.sql`; probe rows and the
  ping URL are configuration, not schema, and are deliberately not in the
  migration because one carries an API key and the other is a credential.

  **NOTHING WAS DEPLOYED. NO EDGE FUNCTION WAS TOUCHED, PUBLISHED OR CHANGED.**

  **THE FOUR PATHS, AND WHAT EACH ONE DOES AND DOES NOT FIRE ON.** Andrew's
  ruling governs this table: *"if he gets an email that something failed he is
  not going to do anything about it"*, so **a check that can cry wolf is worse
  than no check.**

  | path | what it proves | it fires when | it deliberately does NOT fire when |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `homepage` | Netlify is serving a real build | two cycles in a row where the body does not contain `assets/index-` | one slow fetch; a redeploy changing the hash — the assertion is the prefix, not the hash |
  | `booking_start` | the tenant profile the booking page loads first — Postgres, a definer RPC, PostgREST | two cycles where the RPC does not return opening hours | a tenant having odd hours; RLS refusing some *other* table |
  | `booking_availability` | the edge runtime computing real slots | two cycles where the function does not answer `"success":true` | **a fully booked day** — the assertion is on `success`, never on the number of slots, because no free slots is not an outage |
  | `sign_in` | the authentication service is answering | two cycles where it does not identify itself | a wrong password, a locked account, a rate-limited login — **this probe carries no credentials at all**, so no user-specific failure can trip it |

  **AND THREE WOLVES WERE DESIGNED OUT RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE DISCOVERED:**

  - **A response that has not arrived is INCONCLUSIVE, never a failure.**
  - **If nothing could be graded, the ping is WITHHELD rather than sent.** A
    success ping we could not justify is the worst thing available here — a
    monitor reporting green because it did not look. Observed on the very
    first run: `{"ping":"withheld — nothing could be graded this cycle"}`.
  - **The probe body is a template, not a fixture.** A hard-coded future date
    is in the past a few weeks later and a hard-coded duration breaks the day
    somebody reseeds the demo tenant — both would start crying wolf about a
    product that is fine. The date and the duration are substituted each cycle
    from live data.

  **TWO CANDIDATE PROBES WERE KILLED BY MEASURING THEM.** An anonymous read of
  `businesses` and of `services` each answer **200 with `[]`**, because RLS
  refuses them — exactly as 4.4's matrix proved. Either would have been a
  green light for ever. **And the item asks for five paths where only four can
  fail independently:** `/book/demo-detail` is served by the same `index.html`
  as the homepage, so a fifth probe of it could not fail on its own. Said
  rather than faked. What the item calls "a safe database or function path" is
  covered separately by `booking_start` (database) and `booking_availability`
  (function).

  **THE CONTROLLED FAILURE, WHICH IS THE DONE-WHEN.** The homepage probe's
  content assertion was changed to a marker the page cannot contain —
  simulating Netlify serving a build without the app bundle, which is a
  failure that returns **200**, because `_redirects` makes every URL on that
  domain return 200. Then, from the check's own event log:

  - first failing cycle → the prober pinged **ok**, and healthchecks.io stayed
    **up**. **One failure says nothing.** This is the assertion that matters
    most and it is the one a monitor usually gets wrong.
  - second consecutive failing cycle → the prober pinged **`/fail`** with
    `{"failing":["homepage"]}`, healthchecks.io went **up → down**, and the
    email integration to Andrew fired.
  - an incident row was written naming the path and the reason: *"status 200,
    expected 200, body did not contain 'THIS-BUILD-MARKER-CANNOT-EXIST'"*.
  - the assertion was restored → next cycle pinged **ok** → **down → up**, and
    a recovery row was written. healthchecks.io recorded the whole thing as
    **1 downtime, 22 seconds, 99.99% uptime.**

  **THE TOLERANCE LIVES IN THE PROBER, NOT IN healthchecks.io** — healthchecks
  goes down on the first `/fail` it receives, which is correct, because the
  prober is the only thing that knows the difference between slow and broken.

  **TWO REAL EMAILS REACHED ANDREW DOING THIS, AND HERE THEY ARE SO HE DOES
  NOT HAVE TO ASK.** Both are from healthchecks.io, both about the check named
  **`detailing platform — live site paths`**, and both were caused on purpose
  by this work:

  | when (Pacific, 2026-09-23) | what it said | what it was |
  |---|---|---|
  | **21:55** | the check went **DOWN** | the deliberate break — the homepage assertion pointed at a marker the page cannot contain |
  | **21:56** | the check came back **UP** | the assertion restored, one cycle later |

  **Nothing was wrong with the site at any point.** healthchecks.io recorded
  the pair as one incident lasting **22 seconds**. Any later mail about this
  check is real.

  ### AND A SESSION PUT AN API KEY IN A DATABASE COLUMN. IT IS OUT. 2026-09-23

  **Asked directly whether `site_probes.headers` held a key or merely could,
  the answer was the first one.** This session seeded three of the four probe
  rows with the project's publishable API key as a literal value — 208
  characters, plain text, in a table — and then wrote in the migration's own
  comment that the column *"holds an API key"*, which is how a mistake gets
  recorded as though it were a design.

  **IT DOES NOT MATTER THAT IT WAS THE PUBLISHABLE KEY**, the one already
  inside the site's own JavaScript bundle. The rule is absolute and a database
  column is an "anywhere": **a rule with a judgement call in it is not a
  rule**, and the next value somebody decides is "not really secret" will be
  the one that is.

  **WHAT WAS DONE, IN ORDER** —
  `supabase/migrations/20260923050000_probe_headers_hold_no_credential.sql`:

  1. **The value is gone.** Stripped from every row. It was never in git — the
     seeding ran from a scratch script that read the key at run time and the
     migration file never contained it — so the table was the only copy, and
     there is now none. `net.http_request_queue` holds **0 rows** and no
     header of that shape survives in `pg_net` either; checked, not assumed.
  2. **It cannot be put back.** A check constraint refuses any `headers` value
     carrying `apikey` or `Authorization`. **Broken on purpose three ways** —
     an update with `apikey`, an update with `Authorization`, and an insert of
     a fresh row carrying one — and the database refused all three with
     `23514`. **The first attempt at that sabotage was itself wrong and said
     the constraint did nothing**: it used `headers || '{...}'`, and
     `NULL || jsonb` is `NULL` in Postgres, so the update never carried a key
     at all. The check was innocent and the test was broken — which is this
     repo's own warning about breaking a check on purpose, arriving from the
     other direction.
  3. **The reference, not the value.** The row now carries `secret_name`, a
     NAME, pointing at Supabase Vault. The prober resolves it at the moment it
     makes the request into a local variable that is gone when the function
     returns — the same shape the edge functions use with `Deno.env.get`, and
     the same shape `docs/services-and-secrets.md` describes.

  **~~IT IS EMPTY~~ — IT HOLDS ONE SECRET NOW, AND HERE IS WHO PUT IT THERE.**
  `vault.secrets` held **zero** secrets when this was written. **No session
  will put one there.** Provisioning is **Andrew's**, and it was one statement
  he ran himself, with the value never passing through a session:

  ```sql
  select vault.create_secret('<the publishable anon key>', 'site_probe_api_key');
  ```

  **If the stored value ever has to CHANGE, that is a different statement and
  still his.** `vault.create_secret` refuses a name that already exists, so a
  replacement is the update form, by id:

  ```sql
  select vault.update_secret(
    (select id from vault.secrets where name = 'site_probe_api_key'),
    '<the new key>');
  ```

  **HE RAN IT. 2026-09-24, 06:52:29 UTC. THE MONITOR COVERS ALL FOUR PATHS
  NOW, AND THE PARAGRAPH BELOW IS KEPT AS THE STATE IT REPLACED.**

  `site_probe_api_key` exists — **one row in `vault.secrets`, confirmed by
  NAME**. Two full cycles were then forced and watched:

  ```
  {"ping":"ok","graded":4,"failing":[],"skipped":[]}      ×2
  ```

  **`skipped` is empty and `graded` is 4**, where it was 2 and
  `["booking_start","sign_in"]` before. Both new paths returned a **200 with
  real content** — `booking_start` a full set of opening hours out of
  `get_public_business_profile`, `sign_in` GoTrue naming itself
  (`{"version":"v2.197.0","name":"GoTrue",…}`). `consecutive_failures` is **0
  on all four** and neither new probe has ever recorded a failure.

  **`failing: []` WAS NOT TAKEN AS THE ANSWER, AND MUST NOT BE.** `fail_after`
  is 2, so a probe that failed once is absent from `failing` — the "one
  failure says nothing" rule that makes this monitor worth having also makes
  its headline unable to report a first failure. The verdict above comes from
  the **per-probe `consecutive_failures` counters and the response bodies**,
  not from the ping.

  **THE PUBLISHABLE KEY FORMAT WORKED, AND THAT WAS THE OPEN QUESTION.** He
  used a modern **`sb_publishable_`** key, not the legacy `eyJ…` anon JWT, and
  **the publishable one was what was tried first — it was not a fallback.**
  The concern was real: `probe_live_site()` sends the credential in **two
  positions at once**, as `apikey` *and* as `Authorization: Bearer <secret>`,
  and the Bearer position is the one the legacy JWT was designed for, so a
  401 on either of these two probes would have been the key format rather than
  an outage. **It did not happen.** Both endpoints accept the publishable key
  in both positions. **No swap is needed and none was made** — and had one
  been, it would have been Andrew's to run, with `vault.update_secret`, since
  `vault.create_secret` refuses a name that already exists.

  **THE VALUE WAS NEVER READ.** Verification selected `name`, `created_at`
  and `updated_at` from `vault.secrets` and nothing else. `decrypted_secret`
  was not queried, not in full and not as a prefix or a predicate. The key
  format above is known from what Andrew said he pasted and from the probes
  answering 200 — **not from looking.**

  **AND THE CREDENTIAL IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN DECORATIVE**, which is the
  difference between "now covered" and a sentence. Measured directly: both
  paths answer **401 with no credential at all** —
  `POST /rest/v1/rpc/get_public_business_profile` → 401, `GET /auth/v1/health`
  → 401. So before 06:52 these two genuinely could not be probed, and the
  skip was honest rather than a missing feature.

  ---

  **THE STATE THIS REPLACED, KEPT BECAUSE THE DESIGN DECISION IN IT STILL
  GOVERNS:** *until he does, the monitor covers two paths, not four — and it
  says so rather than pretending.* `booking_start` and `sign_in` both need a
  key; `homepage` and `booking_availability` need none. **A missing credential
  is reported as SKIPPED, never as DOWN**, because reporting it as an outage
  would make the monitor lie in order to make provisioning feel urgent — the
  exact wolf this design exists to avoid. And a skip is not silent: `skipped`
  rides on every ping, so it is visible in the check's own event detail.
  Measured before provisioning: `{"ping":"ok","graded":2,"failing":[],
  "skipped":["booking_start","sign_in"]}`.

  **`available-slots` NEEDS NO KEY AT ALL, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING SEPARATELY.**
  Measured: called with no `apikey` header whatsoever it answers 200 with real
  slots, because it is a public function deployed without JWT verification.
  That is the product working as intended — the booking page is public — but
  it had not been written down anywhere.

  **IT SPENDS NONE OF THE SHARED BUDGETS ON `docs/shared-resources.md`.** No

  **`scripts/db-audit.mjs` CAUGHT THIS MIGRATION AND IT WAS RIGHT TO.** Both

  ### BUILT AND PROVED 2026-09-23 — one condition alerts, four are named and left out

  **`watch_tenant_bookability()`, hourly on `pg_cron`, with its own
  healthchecks.io check** — *"detailing platform — a detailer's page stopped
  working"*, one-hour period, three-hour grace. **Its own check on purpose:**
  one detailer's page going quiet must not take down the alarm that says
  whether the whole platform is up. Two different alarms, two different
  sentences. No deploy; no edge function touched.

  **THE ONE THING IT ALERTS ON:** *a detailer who WAS working and has stopped
  being bookable.* "Was working" is carried by one fact — **they have taken at
  least one booking.** That single qualifier is the whole answer to *broken vs
  merely empty*: a business with no services that has never had a booking is
  setting up; one that took bookings last month and has no services today has
  lost something.

  **ALL FIVE CONDITIONS, AND THEY ARE IN FOUR DIFFERENT STATES. THAT
  DISTINCTION IS THE ITEM.** "One of five watched" reads as four forgotten, and
  that is not what happened — but **unbuilt and undistinguishable look
  identical in a roadmap and are not remotely the same thing**, so each is
  named:

  | condition | state | why |
  |---|---|---|
  | **no services** | **WATCHED** | Arm one. Fired, proved, recovered. |
  | **no future availability** | **WATCHED** | Arm two, below. Asked rather than inferred. |
  | **a suspended account** | **BUILT AND DELIBERATELY SILENT** | Not an outage — **the platform did it**, on purpose, for non-payment. Mailing Andrew about a thing Andrew did is the definition of a wolf. Excluded by name in the SQL. |
  | **no coverage area** | **THE PREMISE IS FALSE** | Not hard to distinguish — **it cannot break a booking page at all.** Measured twice: `service_area` is written at signup, read for display and translation, and **nothing in the booking path ever branches on it.** Alerting on it would fire on a normal state, always. Retired rather than deferred. |
  | **a public error** | **NOT BUILT, AND NOT BUILDABLE HERE** | **Nothing in this database records that a visitor saw one.** There is nothing to read. Sentry is the instrument; it needs a DSN from Andrew that does not exist yet. **It belongs to 7.2** and `docs/ops/monitoring.md` § 4 — stated here rather than left as a fifth blank. |

  **A SECOND IMPLEMENTATION IS DECLARED RATHER THAN HIDDEN.** "Not bookable"
  is the product's own definition, from `adminInsight.js`'s `bookability()`.
  `pg_cron` cannot call JavaScript, so two of its three arms are restated in
  SQL. **That is the exact shape 9.1 is**, fixed hours earlier, so it is kept
  as narrow as possible — two counts, no interpretation — and **if
  `bookability()` grows a third reason this will not know.** Written down at
  the moment the cost was incurred.

  **THE FIRST VERSION WOULD HAVE BEEN RED FROM THE HOUR IT SHIPPED, AND ONLY
  RUNNING IT SAID SO.** Its very first sweep — the one meant to establish a
  healthy baseline — pinged `/fail` with `roles-a (no open days)`. `roles-a` is
  a **test fixture** from the roles suite: one booking, one service, no open
  days. It satisfies every rule this sweep has, because the rules were written
  about detailers and **a fixture looks exactly like a detailer in every column

  not exist and then a permanently red alarm. `is_demo` is now excluded
  (`20260923070000`).

  **AND THE HONEST CONSEQUENCE: THIS SWEEP WATCHES ZERO DETAILERS TODAY.** All
  17 active businesses are fixtures except `counter-signup-test-detail`, which
  has never taken a booking. Not because the sweep is broken — because there
  are none. It starts working, with no change of any kind, the first time a

  **WHEN IT IS WATCHING NOBODY IT PINGS `ok` WITH `looked: 0`, AND THAT IS A
  SILENCE CHOSEN WITH ITS EYES OPEN.** Withholding the ping turns the check red
  within its grace and mails Andrew about a monitor with nothing to do — and
  the next red, a real one, then lands in a mailbox that has learned to ignore
  this check. Pinging `ok` keeps it green and puts `looked: 0` in the check's
  own event detail, so the state is printed rather than silent. **If this
  product ever has detailers and it still says `looked: 0`, that is a fault**,
  and the number is in the body so somebody can see it.

  ### ARM TWO — "NO FUTURE AVAILABILITY", ASKED RATHER THAN INFERRED

  **The fifth condition was UNBUILT, not undistinguishable, and the whole
  reason this item stayed open for one more pass is that those two look the
  same in a roadmap.** Arm one catches a detailer with **no open days at all**
  — a structural fact read off `business_hours`. That is not what the item
  names. **A detailer can have seven open days and nothing anybody can book**,
  because slots are computed rather than stored: hours, buffer, slot interval,
  advance windows, vehicle rules, blockouts and existing bookings. Only asking
  produces the answer.

  So it asks. **One call to `available-slots` per detailer per hour**, across
  the next fortnight, alerting only when **no day in the whole window has a
  single slot.** **The window is the guard: nothing on a Tuesday is a Tuesday;
  nothing across fourteen days is a fault.**

  **FOUR WOLVES SHUT OFF, AND THESE ARE WHY IT WILL STILL BE HONEST IN A
  MONTH:**

  1. **The same four front conditions as arm one** — mid-setup, suspended,
     deliberately closed, never having worked. It never fires at somebody
     still building their page.
  2. **A detailer arm one already failed is not asked.** Otherwise one broken
     detailer produces two alarms saying different things about one fact.
  3. **FULLY BOOKED IS SUCCESS, NOT AN OUTAGE.** A detailer booked solid for a
     fortnight has no slots and nothing is wrong. **Any booking starting inside
     the window and the tenant is not alerted on** — one line, and it is the
     entire difference between *"your page is broken"* and *"you are busy"*.
  4. **BLOCKED OUT IS DELIBERATE.** `blockout_dates` is a real feature. Any
     blockout overlapping the window silences this arm for that tenant.
     **THE COST OF THAT CONSERVATISM IS NAMED RATHER THAN HIDDEN:** a detailer
     with one blocked afternoon somewhere in the fortnight **and** a genuine
     fault will not be alerted on. `blockout_dates` carries a `repeat` column,
     so proving blockouts cover *every* day is real arithmetic, and getting it
     subtly wrong points at mailing Andrew about somebody on leave. **Under a
     silence-unless-real ruling that is the right direction to be wrong in**,
     and arm one still covers that tenant for services and hours.

  **AND THE SERVICE TYPE IS READ, NOT ASSUMED.** Asking a drop-off-only
  detailer for mobile slots returns nothing — **the monitor would have
  invented a wolf out of a business working perfectly.** The probe asks for
  whatever that business actually offers.

  **No credential is sent, and that is measured rather than hoped for.**
  `available-slots` is public and deployed without JWT verification: called
  with no `apikey` header at all it answers 200 with real slots. `tenant_watch`
  holds no key.

  **PROVED ON A THROWAWAY DETAILER, AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THE BREAK WAS
  ITSELF WRONG.** `max_advance_days = 0` was **refused by the database** — the
  product will not allow that state, so **a break the product cannot suffer
  proves nothing.** Switched to `min_advance_minutes = 43200`: a thirty-day
  minimum notice, which has **no upper bound** and is a realistic fat-finger.
  Hours intact, nothing blocked, not busy, and no day in the fortnight
  bookable. Measured:

  - first bad grade → **silent**.
  - second consecutive bad grade → alert naming the reason and the window:
    *"nothing bookable in the next 14 days (2026-09-25 to 2026-10-08) — this
    detailer has taken bookings before"*.
  - restored → quiet one cycle later, recovery row written.
  - **Tenant deleted, orphan incident rows cleared**, 16 businesses active,
    nothing suspended.

  **THE PROOF SENT NO MAIL.** The ping was disconnected for its whole duration
  and reconnected afterwards — **six emails was the night's limit and it had
  been reached.** The ping-to-email path this feeds was already proved end to
  end at 22:33 with arm one; what needed proving here was the decision.

- [x] **6.4a — Today is readable offline only while the screen that loaded it
  stays open. Reload it, or leave and come back, and it is blank.**
  Found 2026-10-06 by DP Cowork while building 6.4(a); said in that commit
  rather than hidden. **6.4(a)'s done-when says "on a screen that had already
  loaded" and is met; this is the next thing a detailer in a driveway does.**
  A detailer who switches to Calendar and back, or whose phone reloads the tab
  after it slept, finds an empty Today with a raw network error.

  **Why:** the day's jobs live in the screen's own state (`useBookings`), so
  unmounting Today throws them away. And `app/public/sw.js` is deliberately
  *not* a caching worker (its own header: *"a worker that starts serving stale
  HTML is a far worse bug than the one it was added to fix"*), so a cold load
  with no signal gets no app at all.

  **Two halves, and the second is Andrew's call:**
  1. *Leave and return.* Keep the last good list for the session outside the
     screen, so coming back offline shows it with the same *as of* line.
  2. *Cold reload.* Either an app-shell cache (reverses a stated worker rule,
     and puts customer names and phones on the device) or a plain "no
     connection" page that says the print sheet is the fallback. **A decision,
     not a default; recommendation: leave-and-return now, and for cold reload
     the plain page, because the printed schedule already covers the outage.**

  **Done when:** with the network cut, **(1)** opening Calendar and returning
  to Today shows today's jobs and the *as of* line, and **(2)** a hard reload of
  `/app` shows either the jobs with the line, or the plain no-connection page
  if Andrew chooses that — never a blank screen or a raw *Failed to fetch*. If
  anything is kept on the device, **signing out clears it**, shown by signing
  out and reading it back. **Red proof:** drop the keeping step and (1) goes
  blank.
  *Lane:* A (`app/src`, plus `sw.js` if the cache is chosen).

  **BUILT AND TICKED 2026-10-06, commit `e6302d5` (DP Cowork, Lane A). Andrew's
  standing instruction was to do BOTH halves; the decision and its cost are in
  DECISIONS.md under the same title.**
  * **Leave and return, offline:** Today draws the saved list with *You're
    offline. Showing your jobs as of 4:11 PM.* in **0.1 seconds** (87 to 152ms
    across runs) instead of waiting out the retries for a spinner.
  * **Reload, offline:** the worker starts the app from its cached shell and
    `NoConnection.jsx` shows the saved list with the same line, phone and address
    on each row, and Print for the next day with jobs. **It is no longer the
    sign-in form or *Create your business*** (a failed membership read used to
    fall through to both). Reached in **4.4 seconds** on the weak-signal path
    (Playwright leaves `navigator.onLine` true on a reload, so the browser's own
    offline flag is not what was measured) and at once when the browser says it is
    offline.
  * **Nothing stored:** a plain *No connection* page with a Retry button, not
    blank. Retry with the signal back restores the dashboard and saves the list
    again.
  * **Sign-out clears it:** **0 keys left** after signing out; the stored entry is
    customer names, phones and addresses on the device, which is the cost named in
    DECISIONS.md.
  * **Measured offline on my own fixture business** (its own owner, five jobs,
    deleted afterward), 320 and 1440, `?lite=1`, with the address and forecast
    calls aborted in the browser so the shared hourly address budget was not
    touched: **14 of 14 checks at both widths**, no sideways scroll, console clean

  * **Still true, and said:** a device that has never loaded the dashboard online

## Wave 7 — Sales proof

**VERIFIED AGAINST THE SOFTWARE, 2026-09-20 — the pricing page and the five
examples, read the way the legal pages were: not for prose, but for places the
page says something the product does not do.**

**THE HONEST FRAME FIRST, because it changes what every finding below is
worth: none of these pages has ever been read by somebody deciding whether to
buy.** Zero paying subscriptions, one non-demo business. **So every defect
here is still free to fix** — nobody has been misled, nobody has paid on a
wrong number, and the whole of Wave 7 is a debt that has not yet come due.

**THE ONE SENTENCE THAT SAYS WHY THIS WAVE EXISTS:**

> A stranger reading that page today would be told they get unlimited photos
> and an export, and they would get roughly one photo and no export.

**7.6 IS CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY AND IT IS WORSE THAN ITS OWN LINE.** The item
already records "1 GB total, 10.2 MB promised to each", from the back office.
Reading it out of the database instead — `photo_total_bytes()` is 1 GB and
`photo_tenant_share()` is 100, so the cap is 1 GB ÷ 100 — gives the same
figure, which is the useful part: two independent routes agree. **What the
item does not say is that it is ENFORCED and how small it is in practice.**
`JobPhotos.jsx` refuses the file outright — *"Photo storage is full. Remove
some photos to add more."* — and the `job-photos` bucket accepts a **single
file of up to 10 MB**. **So one photo the product is willing to take uses 98%
of that detailer's entire allowance.** A feature sold as unlimited runs out on
the first job. **Services, bookings and staff logins genuinely are unlimited;
only "photos" is false.** On Andrew's list with both ways out and no
recommendation, because the answer depends on what storage costs him.

**7.7 IS WIDER THAN RECORDED: THE EXPORT IS SOLD IN TWO PLACES.** The item
names the terms and the pricing page. It is also the **home page's** answer to
*"What happens to my customers if I cancel?"* — *"You export them and go. The
list was always yours."* That is arguably the worst of the three, because it
is the direct answer to the question a nervous detailer actually asks. There
is no customer export and no photo export; the only download is the
accountant's CSV of jobs and expenses.

**7.10's `/ex5` ENTRY IS STALE.** It calls the site "Tampa Bay" and the
question about a real company's name is already answered: it is **"Sunglade
Auto Detail"** with an address on a reserved `.example` domain. "Tampa Bay"
survives only as a place — *"Mobile detailing across Tampa Bay"* — which is a
region, not a company. Andrew's list row was closed rather than left for him
to decide something already done.

**THE EXAMPLES DO NOT OVER-PROMISE, AND THIS WAS THE QUESTION WORTH ASKING.**
A real tenant site is built bespoke by an agent following
`docs/tenant-site-kit.md`, so a hand-built example IS the product rather than
a picture of it. Every headline feature on `/examples` maps to something
`get_public_business_profile` actually returns, checked key by key:

| What an example demonstrates | What backs it |
|---|---|
| ex4's before-and-after slider | `gallery_images.before_url` / `after_url`, published from the job screen by `publishToGallery` |
| ex5's "pick your vehicle and the prices change" | `services.vehicle_size_adjustments` and `vehicle_sizes` |
| ex3's "every price on the page" | `services` with `price`, `price_is_from`, `duration_minutes` |
| ex2's step-by-step walkthrough | `services`, `faqs`, `hours` |
| ex1's Work and Prices as real tabs | a build choice; the agent writes the pages |

**And the claim on the index page holds too.** It says *"Every price and time
on these is a placeholder. On a real detailer's site each one comes live from
their own dashboard."* The examples' booking sections are indeed drawings —
annotated `data-from="core.js stepsFor(addOns)"`, with no form, no iframe and
no request — and the kit makes the live half a rule rather than an aspiration:
*"A price, service, hour or plan hard-coded into the site — **No, and this is
the one hard no.**"*

**One framing point rather than a defect:** `/examples` describes ex3 as *"in
three colors you can switch between"*, which reads as a feature of that site.
It is a design choice Andrew was offered three ways; a real tenant has one
brand colour from their dashboard. An agent could build a switcher, so nothing
is promised that cannot be delivered — but the sentence describes an artefact
of the review rather than a tenant feature.

**7.12'S BLANK SECOND IS WORSE THAN "BLANK" AND IT NEARLY PRODUCED A FALSE
FINDING.** The item records that the pricing page is blank for about a second.
**It is not blank — for that moment it shows the LIST prices**, because the
founding lookup has not answered and the code deliberately does not render a
founding price optimistically. A read taken in that window showed *"$600 a
year"* in the terms against *"$40 a month"* in the ladder — a money
contradiction inside the AB 2863 disclosure block, quoted straight from the
page, and completely untrue. Re-probing the DOM after it settled gave
`$400` / `$40` / `$50` and a `$120` worked exit fee, consistent throughout.
**`docs/gotchas.md` carries it: a page read before its data resolves will hand
you a confident contradiction between two numbers that never disagreed.**

**AND THE PAGE DOES EXPLAIN ITSELF**, which was the third question and the one
that needed evidence rather than an opinion. In reading order: *"Two plans.
Three ways to pay."* → *"FOUNDING PRICE — 3 of 3 spots left. It is locked for
the life of the account and never rises while that account stays open. When
the last one goes, this page shows the standard prices instead."* → the build
fee, the monthly, the saving → *"BEFORE YOU PAY — The terms, in full. Not a
link to a policy page. This is all of it."* → eight plain clauses including a
worked example: *"On 12 months at $40 a month, walking away halfway through
costs $120."* **The one place it can be misread** is the summary strip, where
`TO BUILD IT $499 once · THEN $40 a month · SAVE ON THE YEAR $80 a year` puts
two prices and one saving in identical formatting. The label says "SAVE ON",
so it is defensible; named for whoever owns that screen rather than changed.

**NOTHING IN `app/src` WAS EDITED.** Every finding that needs a screen change
is written down for its owner, and the two that are promises about the product
rather than wording went to Andrew.

     plan rate. **Nine levers, all shown.**
  2. **Before the work** — the detailer may send a new price.

     that is a genuinely strong guarantee nobody was claiming.

     `final_amount = total_price + Σ(lines)`; and **`amountDueCents()` returns
     `final_amount ?? total_price`**, so the card charge follows the
     detailer's figure. Its own comment: *"the detailer's agreed final amount
     beats the original quote here exactly as it does everywhere."*
     **No customer consent step.** The invoice itemises the lines afterwards.
